opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people often treat these as being in tension, but I don't really see them that way. The way I'd put it is that "smooth" and "fast" are different axes. When I say I expect capabilities to develop continuously, I mean that you don't get a sudden discontinuity where one day you have a system that's roughly as useful as today's systems and the next day you have something that's radically transformative, with nothing in between. But that's completely compatible with things getting very fast at some point.

So take the intelligence explosion story: AI systems get good enough at AI research that they start speeding up AI progress, which makes the systems better at AI research, and you get this feedback loop. I think that's actually pretty plausible. But if you imagine how it plays out, the first systems that help with AI research are only somewhat helpful. They automate some fraction of the work, maybe they write a bunch of code or run experiments, and that speeds things up by, say, 10% or 30%. Then the next generation is a bit more helpful, and so on. You get something that looks like an exponential, or even super-exponential, curve, but it's still a curve. There's no point where it jumps.

The intuition behind smoothness is basically that there are lots of people pushing on AI, and if some capability is economically valuable, people will build crappier versions of it before they build the good version. So before you get an AI that can do all of AI research, you'll get one that can do a quarter of it, and that's itself a big deal that people will notice and invest in.

Where it matters is in what you expect the world to look like going in. In a continuous world, by the time the feedback loop gets really intense, we've probably already seen a lot of pretty impressive AI systems, the world has already been transformed in significant ways, and, importantly, we've had chances to see earlier versions of the problems we're worried about. That's not a guarantee that we'll handle them well, but it does mean we're more likely to get warning shots, and our alignment techniques can be iterated on with systems that are close to the frontier.

I'll admit the honest caveat: "smooth" can still mean the final stretch happens over months rather than years, and in that case the practical difference from a discontinuous takeoff shrinks a lot. You don't get much time to react if the whole process compresses. So I don't think continuity is a reason for complacency. It mostly changes where I'd focus: less on "we get one shot at a system that appears from nowhere," and more on making sure that during the run-up we're actually building the tools, the institutions, and the alignment techniques that will scale as things accelerate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people hear "continuous" or "smooth" and they interpret it as "slow," and that's not really what I mean. When I say capabilities develop smoothly, I mean that there aren't these big discontinuous jumps where one day you have a system that's basically a toy and the next day it's a superintelligence. You get gradual improvement, and each generation of systems looks somewhat like a better version of the previous one.

But smooth doesn't rule out fast. You can have an exponential, or even a hyperbolic curve, that's perfectly continuous and still ends up going very quickly. So the intelligence explosion story, where AI systems start contributing to AI research and that feedback loop speeds things up, is actually pretty compatible with the continuous view. I'd expect that if we get something like that, it'll look like: AI systems become somewhat useful for research, then more useful, then they're doing most of the work, and the rate of progress keeps increasing along the way. There's no single moment where it "goes foom." It's just that the slope keeps getting steeper.

Where I'd push back on the classic intelligence explosion framing is more on the specifics. The old story was often something like one system in a basement recursively self-improving over a weekend, and nobody outside notices until it's over. I think that's pretty unlikely. Partly because progress right now seems to depend a lot on compute and data and large-scale engineering, not just on having a clever idea, and those things take time and are visible. And partly because the systems that would be doing the automating are built by the same organizations that are already pushing the frontier, so you'd expect the acceleration to show up in the broader ecosystem, not in one isolated system.

So the practical upshot for me is: I do think there's a real chance that the last few years before transformative AI are much faster than the years before them, and that matters a lot for how much time we have to react. But I also expect we'll see it coming, in the sense that there will be earlier, weaker versions of the thing that we can study, test our alignment techniques on, and learn from. That's actually a big part of why I'm somewhat more optimistic than some people. If you believed in a sharp discontinuity, you'd have to get everything right in advance with no empirical feedback. If it's continuous, even if fast, you get to iterate. The worry is just whether the iteration happens fast enough relative to the acceleration.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think those are necessarily in tension. You can have a process where each individual improvement is fairly small, but those improvements make the system better at producing further improvements. So the whole thing accelerates, potentially very dramatically, without there being a particular point where capabilities suddenly jump discontinuously.

The question is how strong that feedback loop is. If you make an AI system a little smarter, how much faster can it do AI research? And how much does that research actually improve the next system? There could be bottlenecks from running experiments, getting more compute, or just finding that further improvements become harder.

So I’d distinguish smoothness from slowness. Saying that capabilities develop smoothly doesn’t, by itself, tell you that going from roughly human-level AI to much more capable AI takes decades. It could be quite fast. But it also doesn’t establish that an intelligence explosion will happen—you need an additional argument about how powerful that feedback loop will be.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think those are necessarily in tension. You can have a process where every individual improvement is fairly small, but the improvements compound very quickly. If better AI systems let you do AI research faster, that gives you better AI systems, which lets you do research faster still. That could produce a very rapid increase in capabilities without any particular step being discontinuous.

So I’d distinguish smoothness from speed. Saying capabilities develop smoothly doesn’t mean that they develop slowly, or that we necessarily get years to react to each new development.

The question is how strong that feedback loop is. How much of AI research can you automate? How much does making the researcher more capable actually accelerate progress? Are you bottlenecked on running experiments, getting more compute, or collecting evidence from the world? Those things could substantially limit the acceleration.

So I take an intelligence explosion seriously as a possibility. But I don’t think it follows just from the observation that AI will eventually be able to improve AI. You need an argument about the strength of the feedback and the timescales involved.
